# The Gospel of Perdition Gulch

## I. Now

The sickness came the way most things came to Perdition Gulch—on a wind from the east, carrying dust and the promise of ruin.

Constance Bellweather noticed it first, because Constance Bellweather noticed everything first. She was standing at the window of the Assayer's Office, which had not assayed anything in eleven years but which served as the council's unofficial chambers, and she was watching the Tuesday coach rattle down the gulch road when the driver's face escaped her.

Not his name. She had never known his name. But his face—the precise configuration of pockmarks along his left jaw, the place where his lower lip cracked every winter, the distance between his pupils measured to the fraction of a hair—all of this, which had been filed and catalogued and cross-referenced in the vast and flawless architecture of her memory since the first time she'd seen him drive the 2:15 from Silver Creek on a September afternoon in 1879, simply was not there.

She stood very still. She breathed in. She breathed out.

She tried to recall the face of her mother, dead these forty years.

It was there. Every line, every broken capillary, the small scar above the eyebrow where a porcelain cup had struck bone—all present, all vivid, all impossibly preserved.

She tried the driver again.

Nothing. Or rather—something. A smudge. The general impression of a man. The kind of memory that ordinary people carried, imprecise and porous and riddled with invention. The kind of memory that made her skin crawl.

Constance Bellweather had not had an ordinary memory since the age of three, when she had looked at her father's pocket watch and understood that she could read back every digit on its face hours later, days later, years later—not from effort, not from practice, but because the world wrote itself upon her in indelible ink and nothing, nothing, was ever lost.

Until now.

She said nothing to the others. This was her first mistake, though not her worst.

---

## II. Then

They found each other the way iron filings find a magnet—slowly, then all at once, drawn by a force none of them could name and all of them could feel.

Silas Cain arrived first, in the final bitter winter of 1862, when Perdition Gulch was nothing more than a mining camp clinging to the side of a worthless mountain like a barnacle on a rotting hull. He had deserted from the Confederate Army after the Battle of Antietam, where a Union bayonet had opened him from navel to sternum and a field surgeon had pronounced him dead and moved on to the next screaming boy. Twelve hours later, Silas Cain sat up on the pile of corpses where they'd thrown him, his wound already closing, his uniform stiff with blood that had forgotten how to keep flowing, and he looked at the carnage of the cornfield around him and understood that he was not meant to die in that place.

He was not, as far as he could determine, meant to die at all.

He had tested this theory with the methodical patience of a man who had nothing left to lose. A knife across the forearm: closed in an hour. A bullet through the thigh, self-administered with whiskey and a leather strap between his teeth: healed by morning. A fall from a cliff outside Perdition Gulch that should have shattered every bone below his waist: three days of agony, and then he walked.

The pain, he wanted people to understand, was not diminished. The pain was every bit as absolute as it would be for anyone. His body simply chose, each time, to continue.

Constance came next, in 1865, riding the same wave of westward migration that brought the defeated and the desperate to every godforsaken hole in the territories. She had been a governess in Philadelphia. She had been a typesetter's assistant. She had been a bookkeeper, a seamstress, a teacher in a schoolhouse that burned down with suspicious regularity after the parents learned she was letting their daughters read. She had been many things, and she remembered every single one of them—every face, every slight, every contract and column of figures and passage of scripture and line of poetry and blade of grass she had ever looked upon—and the weight of it had driven her as far west as the roads would take her.

She came to Perdition Gulch because it was the last place before nowhere.

The twins arrived in 1871, and the child in 1873, and by then the magnet had done its work. The five of them sat in the back room of the Assayer's Office and looked at one another across a table, and for the first time in each of their lives, they were not alone in what they were.

"So," Constance said. She had, by then, read every medical text available in three territories. "What are we?"

Nobody answered. The question hung in the air like gunsmoke.

The child, Ezra, who was seven and feral and had been found sleeping in a horse trough, looked at each of them in turn with eyes too old for his face. Then he said, in a voice he rarely used because other people's thoughts were so much louder:

"Scared."

---

## III. Now

Silas noticed three weeks after Constance, because Silas was a man who avoided noticing things whenever possible. He had built a life from the raw materials of deliberate ignorance—drinking enough to dull the edges, fighting enough to feel something other than the sick certainty of his own permanence, and healing enough to start the cycle again.

But when Hector Briggs caught him across the knuckles with a bottle during a disagreement over cards in the Lucky Chance Saloon, and the cuts were still there at dawn, Silas sat on the edge of his cot and held his hand up to the light and watched the blood dry brown on his skin and felt something he had not felt in twenty-five years.

Fear.

Not the distant, philosophical fear of a man contemplating his own strangeness. The intimate, bowel-loosening fear of a man who has just remembered he is mortal.

He wrapped his hand. He told himself it was a slow night, that's all, a tired night, a night when the body took longer than usual to do what the body always did. He told himself this while his pulse hammered against his wrist, fast and fragile and suddenly precious.

By noon, the cuts had closed. But they had taken nine hours, and nine hours was longer than any wound had ever taken, and Silas Cain—who had survived a bayonet through the belly, a dozen bullets, a cliff, two snakebites, a knife fight in Tucson that had removed most of his left ear (it grew back, pink and tender as a newborn's), and a particularly determined hanging in the town of Redemption, Kansas—Silas Cain started to pack.

---

The narrator must pause here to say something about the nature of Perdition Gulch, because the town itself is a character in this story, or perhaps more accurately a patient, and its diagnosis is relevant.

Picture a canyon, narrow and deep, cut into red rock by a river that stopped running seven years ago. Picture buildings the color of dried blood, built from the stone of the canyon walls, laid out along a single street that runs east to west because the canyon permits nothing else. At the eastern end, the road climbs up and out toward Silver Creek and eventually civilization. At the western end, the canyon narrows to a crevice barely wide enough for a man on horseback, and beyond that lies desert, and beyond that lies nothing anyone has ever returned from to describe.

For twenty years, the five of them had held this town the way a hand holds water—gently, carefully, knowing that the slightest tremor would spill it all.

Constance kept the records. Not the official records—those were maintained by the town clerk, a nearsighted man named Parsons who couldn't have caught a discrepancy in his own ledger with both hands and a magnifying glass. Constance kept the real records: the ones in her head. She knew who owed what to whom, who had lied under oath, who had sold what to which company for how much, and she knew it not because she had investigated but because she had seen it—a glance at a letter left open on a desk, a passing look at a manifest on the loading dock, a single overhearing of a conversation through a thin hotel wall—and she had never forgotten any of it. This perfect knowledge made her, in effect, the law.

Silas kept the peace. This was simpler. In a town where disputes were settled with lead and liquor, a man who could not be killed was a useful deterrent. He had been shot in the Lucky Chance on six separate occasions, and each time he had pulled the bullet from his own flesh at the bar, laid it on the counter next to his whiskey, and looked at his assailant with the weary eyes of a man being asked the same stupid question for the thousandth time. Word traveled. Disputes settled themselves.

Ezra, who was no longer a child but had never quite become an adult—Ezra kept the secrets. He sat on the porch of the Assayer's Office and whittled sticks into shapes that troubled passing horses, and he listened to the thoughts of everyone who walked past, and he told the others what was being planned before it was done. A robbery at the bank. An ambush on the coach road. A railroad agent bribing the territorial commissioner. Ezra heard it all, the ceaseless roar of human intention, and he filtered it through a mind that had learned, out of pure necessity, to distinguish between the thoughts people entertained and the thoughts people meant.

And the twins—

The twins are harder to explain.

---

## IV. Then

Mirabel and Josephine Alcott were born in a farmhouse outside of Lawrence, Kansas, in 1849, and they came into the world screaming with one voice from two mouths. This is not metaphor. This is the precise physiological reality of what the Alcott twins were: one mind expressed through two bodies, one consciousness stretched across two skulls like a canvas across a frame, each body a hand on the same instrument.

They learned, as children, to simulate separateness. Mirabel would say "I" and mean the body on the left. Josephine would say "I" and mean the body on the right. In company, they took turns speaking, pretending to think different thoughts, manufacturing small disagreements and preferences—Mirabel liked her eggs soft, Josephine liked them hard; Mirabel favored blue, Josephine favored green—to create the illusion of two people where there was, in the deepest and most fundamental sense, only one.

This deception was exhausting and, in their private estimation, degrading. They had tried, once, to explain the truth to their mother, and their mother had taken them to a minister, and the minister had prayed over them for six hours and then recommended an asylum in St. Louis, and after that the twins kept their own counsel.

They came to Perdition Gulch because Ezra heard their thoughts from two hundred miles away—two bodies broadcasting the same signal, like two telegraph stations sending the same message simultaneously—and he told Constance, and Constance sent a letter to their boarding house in Denver, and the letter said simply: *We know what you are. We are like you. Come home.*

They had never had a home. They came.

In the council, the twins served as the fulcrum—the tiebreaker, the mediator, the steady center around which the others orbited. Because they had lived their entire lives as a negotiation between two bodies and one will, they understood compromise at a level the others could not. When Silas wanted to solve a problem with violence and Constance wanted to solve it with information and Ezra warned that neither approach would work, the twins sat between them and found the third path, the one that required no blood and no leverage and no betrayal, only patience. Only presence. Only the trick of being in two places at once.

For twenty years, this worked.

Then came the night of the Kramer party.

---

## V. Now

It was Ezra who confirmed what Constance suspected and Silas feared. He came to the Assayer's Office on a Thursday evening in October, when the air smelled of woodsmoke and the coming winter, and he sat down across from Constance and looked at her with the flat, vacant eyes he wore when the thoughts were very loud, and he said:

"It's quieting down."

Constance, who had spent the last three weeks pretending nothing was wrong, set down her pen. She had taken to writing things in a journal—a physical, paper journal, with ink and binding and pages that could be torn and burned—because she no longer trusted the architecture of her own mind. Three days ago, she had failed to recall the face of the Silver Creek banker. Yesterday, she had lost the text of a letter she'd read in 1881. This morning, she had stood in front of the mirror and noticed, with a horror so profound it registered as calm, that she could no longer remember what she had looked like at twenty.

"Define quieting," she said.

"I can still hear them. Everyone. But it's—" He pressed his palms against his temples, a gesture she had seen him make ten thousand times, always in the same way, except today his hands were shaking. "It's like they're moving away. Like I'm hearing them from the bottom of a well."

"When did it start?"

"Two months ago. Maybe three."

Constance calculated. Two or three months ago placed the onset squarely in August. She tried to recall what had happened in August and found, for the first time in her life, that she could not easily access the relevant data. She had to search for it, fumbling through her memory like a clerk hunting through filing cabinets, and the act of searching was so foreign, so grotesquely normal, that she nearly wept.

"Silas?" she asked.

"Still healing. But slower. He thinks I don't know he's been testing it—cutting himself with his razor every morning, timing how long it takes. He thinks I can't hear him counting the minutes." A pause. "I can still hear him. For now."

"The twins?"

Ezra's face did something complicated and terrible. "That's why I'm here."

---

## VI. Then

The Kramer party came through Perdition Gulch on the fourteenth of March, 1873—thirty-one men, women, and children heading west through the canyon on their way to the California coast, led by a Swiss-German patriarch named Johann Kramer who had the eyes of a prophet and the organizational skills of a drowned rat.

They stopped in Perdition Gulch to resupply. They were short on water, shorter on sense, and they intended to push through the western canyon into the desert beyond, despite the fact that it was still winter, despite the fact that the route was unmarked and uncharted, despite the fact that every person in town told them they were heading into their own graves.

Johann Kramer smiled his prophet's smile and said God would provide.

This is the point in the story where it becomes necessary to talk about the Comanche.

Not the nation as a whole—the Comanche were by 1873 a shattered people, driven onto reservations, starving, dying of diseases they had no name for. But in the canyons west of Perdition Gulch, a small band of warriors under a chief the whites called Red Knife had established a territory that the US Army alternately denied existed and refused to enter, and they did not appreciate settlers passing through their land, and they had, over the previous eighteen months, made this displeasure clear in ways that left very little ambiguity.

Ezra heard it first. He was seven years old, sitting on the porch of the Assayer's Office, and he heard the thoughts of the scouts two miles up the western canyon, and what they were thinking was: *The white wagons are in the pass. Tonight.*

He told Constance. Constance told Silas. Silas told the twins. They gathered in the back room, and they argued, and the argument lasted four hours, and during those four hours, thirty-one people made camp at the western mouth of the canyon, unaware that the rocks above them contained men with very old grievances and very sharp knives.
